Empirical Research Plan:  Rural Bank Branch Expansion, 1961-2000  

==================================================================
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------------
Main design: Difference-in-Differences (two-way fixed effects) complemented by a Bartik-style Instrumental Variable.  

Why DID?  
• The policy was rolled out nationally but generated heterogeneous, time-varying “doses” of treatment across states.  
• We observe the same states before and after the expansion ⇒ panel DID exploits within-state changes relative to states that experienced smaller mandated increases.  

Why add an IV?  
• Banks did not open rural branches at random; hard-to-observe economic prospects could drive both branch openings and poverty reduction.  
• The 1977 “1 urban : 4 rural” licensing rule creates plausibly exogenous variation: states with larger pre-1977 urban branch bases were mechanically forced to open more rural branches once the rule began.  
→ Instrument = (pre-1977 urban branches per capita) × (post-1977 dummy) (“shift-share/Bartik”).

Econometric sequence  
a) Baseline TWFE DID with continuous treatment (rural branches per 100,000 pop).  
b) Event-study of dynamic effects.  
c) 2SLS where first stage uses the Bartik instrument.  
d) Robustness: stacked DID (Sun & Abraham, 2021) to alleviate TWFE heterogeneity bias.

==================================================================
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
T_st = Rural bank branches per 100,000 population in state s year t.

Continuous “dose”, but we will often interpret the policy shock of 1977-1990 as the key treatment episode.

Instrument (Z_st)  
Z_st = UrbanBranches1961-1976_s / Pop1961_s × Post1977_t.  
States with higher pre-policy urban branch density are more “exposed”.

Control group / counterfactual  
States with low ex-ante exposure serve as implicit controls; the FE framework nets out common national shocks. In event-study graphs, the control is the average of all other states in each pre-event year.

Treatment timing  
Policy phase-in: 1977-1990. We code Post_t=1 for 1977–1990 (or until 2000 for long-run effects). Event time k = t – 1976.

==================================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel-trends (DID).  
Absent the mandated expansion, poverty trajectories in high-exposure and low-exposure states would have moved in parallel.  
Plausibility: Before 1977, branch growth was demand-driven; we can test for parallel pre-trends with an event-study.

A2. Exclusion (IV).  
Conditional on state and year FE, the interaction instrument affects poverty only through induced rural branches, not via other channels.  
Plausibility: The licensing rule linked rural branches mechanically to historic urban branches; those historic urban levels are predetermined.

A3. No differential anticipation.  
States could not strategically change poverty statistics before 1977 in response to the forthcoming rule. Given surprise announcement and administrative nature, plausible.

A4. Stable unit treatment value (no cross-state spillovers).  
Reasonable because banking services are largely consumed locally; we will test robustness by dropping bordering states.

==================================================================
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Concurrent reforms (e.g., Green Revolution, IRDP).  
Mitigation: control for state-specific agricultural yield shocks, public spending, and other major program dummies; include state×sector trends.

T2. Selective branch placement within states (endogenous micro-location).  
Mitigation: instrument; add state×year FE in robustness to soak up within-state shocks; cluster SEs at state level.

T3. Migration / composition changes.  
Mitigation: use poverty ratios computed from NSS household surveys, which are residence-based; control for net migration rates; show results on alternative outcomes (agri wages) that are less sensitive to migration.

==================================================================
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # TWFE & 2SLS
library(did)         # event-study (Callaway-Sant'Anna)
library(bacondecomp) # pre-trend check

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
dt <- fread("rural_banking_state_panel_1961_2000.csv")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
dt[, rural_br_pc := 100000 * rural_branches / population]
dt[, urban_pre_pc  := 100000 * urban_branches_pre1977 / pop1961]  # pre-policy exposure
dt[, post77        := as.integer(year >= 1977)]
dt[, instrument    := urban_pre_pc * post77]

# Poverty outcomes
dt[, pov_rate  := poverty_headcount]      # %
dt[, gini      := income_gini]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Baseline TWFE DID
did_fe <- feols(pov_rate ~ rural_br_pc | state + year,
                data = dt, cluster = ~state)
summary(did_fe)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Event-study (Callaway-Sant'Anna stacked)
cs <- att_gt(yname = "pov_rate",
             tname = "year",
             idname = "state",
             gname = "first_big_jump_year",  # pre-defined adoption year
             xformla = ~1,
             data = dt)
es  <- aggte(cs, type = "dynamic")
ggdid(es)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. 2SLS with Bartik instrument
iv_fe <- feols(pov_rate ~ 1 | state + year | rural_br_pc ~ instrument,
               data = dt, cluster = ~state)
summary(iv_fe)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Robustness: placebo outcome (urban poverty) & state-specific trends
placebo <- feols(urban_pov_rate ~ rural_br_pc | state + year + state[year],
                 data = dt, cluster = ~state)
summary(placebo)
```

==================================================================
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory suggests that access to formal credit and savings reduces borrowing costs, smooths consumption, and finances productive investment. Therefore:  

• Direction: Rural branch expansion should lower poverty headcount and (ambiguously) reduce inequality.  
• Magnitude (prior): A one-standard-deviation increase (~0.8 branches per 100k) might reduce the poverty rate by 1–1.5 p.p., roughly 3-5 % of the 1970s mean.

==================================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
------------------------------------------------------------------
C1 – Clear treatment and timing: 1  
C2 – Parallel pre-trends verified: 0.5 (needs to be shown)  
C3 – No anticipation: 0.5 (likely but not provable)  
C4 – No spillovers/SUTVA: 0.5 (possible credit flows across borders)  
C5 – No contemporaneous shocks correlated with treatment: 0.5  

Total = 3.0 / 5.
